transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad you could make it in today. What brings you to the clinic?

I keep getting stuck redoing the same checks and routines over and over at work, even when I know they’re unnecessary, and it’s starting to derail my projects and my life. I'm a mechanical engineer, and while I've always been detail-oriented, this has gotten to a point where I just can't seem to stop myself.

When you feel compelled to repeat these checks, is it driven by specific, unwanted thoughts or fears of something bad happening if you don't do them, or is it more about a general need for things to be perfectly orderly and correct?

It is definitely driven by specific, unwanted thoughts. I get these looping fears that if I miss even a tiny detail, like a minor tolerance error, a part will fail down the line and someone will get hurt. Even though I know it's irrational, those images loop in my head and force me to keep checking.
How much time would you say you spend on these unwanted thoughts and checking behaviors on an average day?

It easily takes up several hours of my day. A single checking cycle on a CAD file or email can eat up an hour without me even realizing it, and because I do this repeatedly, I end up staying at the office past midnight and skipping my usual evening routines.
How long have these looping fears and the need to repeatedly check things been happening on most days?

This all started about a year ago during a major product rollout at work. I was suddenly tasked with coordinating multiple design teams under very tight deadlines, and that's when these looping fears and repetitive checks really took over.
Do you try to resist these thoughts or checking behaviors when they happen? Also, does performing the checks bring you any actual pleasure, or does it just temporarily relieve your anxiety?

I'm not quite sure how to answer that, and I haven't really thought about it in terms of pleasure. I just know that I feel incredibly compelled to do these checks, and I can't seem to stop myself when the urge hits.
When you finish performing these checks, do you feel a temporary sense of relief or a reduction in your anxiety, even if it only lasts for a short time?
I'm not entirely sure if it actually brings me relief or lowers my anxiety. It feels more like I'm just driven by a constant, relentless urge to keep checking, and the worry is always right there.
Do you recognize these looping fears and thoughts as coming from your own mind, rather than being put there by some outside force, and are they deeply distressing to you?

Yes, I definitely recognize them as my own thoughts, even though I know they are completely irrational and I can't shut them out. They are incredibly distressing and exhausting because they feel entirely out of my control and are seriously disrupting my work, sleep, and personal life.
Do you ever try to fight or resist the urge to perform these checks, even if you find it extremely difficult or usually end up doing them anyway?

I haven't really thought about trying to actively fight the urges, so I'm not entirely sure. I just feel completely overwhelmed when they happen and end up doing the checks anyway because the whole process feels so out of my control.
Do you ever try to ignore, suppress, or push away those frightening thoughts about parts failing and people getting hurt, even if you find it impossible to do so?

Yes, I constantly try to push those thoughts away and tell myself they are irrational, but I find it impossible to shut them out. It is incredibly frustrating to try to ignore those looping images of parts failing and people getting hurt, only for them to keep forcing their way back into my mind anyway.

latest_inference.note: The patient exhibits both prominent obsessional thoughts (fear of design failure and harm to others) and compulsive behaviors (excessive checking of CAD files and emails), which have been present for a year and cause significant distress and impairment. The thoughts are recognized as the patient's own, are unpleasantly repetitive, and the patient actively tries to push them away (resistance). This fully satisfies the ICD-10 criteria for F42.2 (Mixed obsessional thoughts and acts). No further questioning is required.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with both prominent obsessions (intrusive, ego-dystonic fears of design failure causing harm) and compulsions (excessive, repetitive checking of CAD files and emails) that consume several hours daily. These symptoms have been present for approximately one year, cause significant distress, and interfere greatly with work and personal life. Because both obsessive thoughts and compulsive acts are present and neither clearly dominates, F42.2 (Mixed obsessive thoughts and acts) is the most accurate diagnosis.
